days.title: Ontology Building Blocks: Object Types, Links, Interfaces and Shared Properties

concepts.heading: Model the Workflow Before Designing Screens
concepts.body: The exam guide asks application developers to model meaningful objects and links with stable identity first, and only then design the interface on top of that model. An object type represents a real entity or event such as Equipment, Inspection or Order, its properties hold the attributes, and link types express the relationships between them. If the model is wrong, every Workshop module, Function and Action built on it inherits the problem. Starting from screens tends to produce object types shaped around one page instead of around the business. In scenario questions, an answer that fixes the model is usually stronger than one that patches the user interface.

concepts.heading: Events and Attributed Relationships Become Object Types
concepts.body: When something happens between entities and carries its own data, such as an inspection with a date, result and notes, model it as its own object type with a stable key and many-to-one links to each participant. History then becomes a simple link traversal, for example from a pump to its inspections sorted by date. The same applies to many-to-many relationships that carry attributes: an Assignment holding role and allocation between Employee and Project, or an Enrollment holding term and grade between Student and Course. Time-bounded relationships, such as which driver drove which truck and when, follow the same pattern with start and end times, and the current state is derived from the dated objects. Alternatives like parallel list properties on one object, or a single object overwritten in place, lose history and break ordering.

concepts.heading: Interfaces for a Shared Shape
concepts.body: An interface declares a common set of properties that several object types implement, so applications and Actions can treat those types uniformly. For example, Vehicle, Drone and Vessel all have a location, a status and an operator, so a dispatch application can list them together and one Assign Operator Action can work on any of them through the interface. Interfaces also fit related entities that share a core but differ in detail, such as auto and home coverages modelled as separate object types implementing a common Coverage interface. They are the cure for an overly broad catch-all type with dozens of mostly empty properties: split it into specific types and put the shared properties on an interface. The clearest reason to add an interface is several types whose shared shape consumers want to treat the same way.

concepts.heading: Shared Properties and Value Types
concepts.body: A shared property is defined once and used by several object types, so an attribute such as priority means the same thing on Ticket, Task and Incident. A value type constrains the allowed values, for example a fixed list of official jurisdiction codes, so invalid values are rejected at the source rather than reconciled later. This matters most when different teams own the object types, because one definition prevents each team drifting to its own spelling or code list. If two teams want different wording for the same status values, keep one stable stored value set and let each module display its own labels. Stored values stay stable; presentation adapts in the interface layer.

concepts.heading: Keep Core Types Focused and Avoid Duplicates
concepts.body: When one new application needs many rarely used attributes, put them in a linked object type (for example a CustomerProfileDetail linked to Customer) instead of bloating a core type that many applications depend on. When two teams have each created their own object type for the same entity, such as two Customer types, reports disagree and links point to one or the other. The fix is to consolidate on one type with a stable key and migrate links, user edits and applications in a planned way. Keeping parallel copies and reconciling them in reports only hides the problem. The guide consistently favours one clear, shared model over local copies.

examPoints: When a scenario describes several object types that share a shape and must be listed or acted on together, prefer an interface implemented by each type over a merged catch-all type or one duplicated Action per type.

When a scenario needs one attribute with the same meaning and allowed values across object types owned by different teams, prefer a shared property constrained by a value type over per-team definitions or after-the-fact reconciliation.

quiz.q: A library application records each loan of a book to a member, with loan, due and return dates, and staff need every book's loan history. What should represent a loan?
choices: A Loan object type with its own key, linked many-to-one to Book and to Member
A list of borrower names stored as a property on the Book object
A single current-borrower property on Book that is overwritten at each checkout
A separate Book object type for each member who has borrowed it
quiz.explain: A loan is an event with its own attributes and two participants, so it becomes its own object type with links; history is then a traversal from Book to its Loans, while lists or overwritten properties lose history.

quiz.q: Pump, Valve and Compressor object types each have a serial number, a site and a last-service date. One maintenance table must list all three, and one Schedule Service Action must work on any of them. What should the developer add?
choices: One merged Equipment object type holding every property of all three, most of them empty
A separate copy of the Schedule Service Action for each object type
An interface with the shared properties, implemented by all three object types
A separate module per object type, each linked from a landing page
quiz.explain: An interface lets consumers treat several types with a shared shape uniformly, so one table and one Action cover all three; a sparse catch-all type and per-type copies both add maintenance without fixing the model.

days.recap: Model entities, events and relationships before screens: events and attributed relationships become their own linked object types, interfaces unify types with a shared shape, and shared properties with value types keep cross-type attributes consistent.

days.title: Stable Identity, Cardinality, Workflow Assembly and Workflow Lineage

concepts.heading: Stable Primary Keys
concepts.body: Key objects on identifiers that the system of record assigns once and never reuses, such as an HR employee number, not on names, street addresses or codes that a source may reformat. When a key value changes, the platform sees a brand-new object, so user edits and links stay attached to the old key and appear to vanish after a refresh. When several source systems feed one object type and their ids can collide, namespace the key, for example carrier code plus tracking number, and check uniqueness. Changing the key of a heavily used type is a migration, not an edit: map old to new keys, migrate edits and links, update consumers on a branch and validate. Disappearing edits after a source change are a classic symptom of an unstable key.

concepts.heading: Cardinality Must Match the Data
concepts.body: Translate business rules into cardinality carefully: each ticket has at most one agent while an agent handles many tickets is many-to-one from Ticket to Agent, backed by an agent id on the ticket. If a link is configured as one-to-one but some customers really have several accounts, the application shows one account seemingly at random. The fix is to correct the model to one-to-many, verify with counts, and update the consumers that assumed a single value. Many-to-many relationships that carry data become their own object type. The guide asks you to check whether the data actually supports a relationship before you model it.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Links That Look Missing
concepts.body: When linked objects appear blank although the target exists, first compare the foreign key values with the target's primary keys exactly: case, padding, prefixes and formats (for example ACME-C123 against C123). The durable fix is to normalize keys to one agreed format in the pipelines and add a check that links resolve after each build. If the link is blank only for some users, also check whether those users can see the target objects, because an invisible target looks the same as a missing one. Avoid patching the display or adding filters while the underlying data mismatch remains. Fix the key format or the access, whichever the evidence points to.

concepts.heading: Assembling Workflows From the Right Parts
concepts.body: The guide asks you to assemble workflows across Ontology entities, Workshop modules, Functions, Actions and Automate, using each for its role. Workshop modules are where people review and decide, Actions make governed and validated changes, Functions hold reusable logic, and automations handle follow-ups such as notifications, policy checks and calls to external systems after a decision. For example, an adjuster reviews a claim in a module, records a validated decision through an Action, and an automation creates the payment task on approval. Store an AI suggestion and the human-confirmed value in separate properties, with the confirmation written by an Action. Reuse shared Actions, Functions and object types and parameterize modules for regional differences instead of copying them.

concepts.heading: Workflow Lineage for Safe Change and Access Troubleshooting
concepts.body: Workflow Lineage shows which modules, Functions, Actions and automations depend on an object type, property or link type. Check it before renaming, deleting, recomputing or changing the cardinality of a resource, then migrate the consumers (ideally on a branch) or keep the resource. For a change of meaning, add a new property, migrate consumers deliberately and retire the old property later instead of redefining it in place. Lineage also answers audit questions such as which applications and automations can change Contract objects and through which Actions. When a user sees empty data in a module, lineage gives the full dependency path so you can check access at each layer and fix the exact one that denies.

examPoints: When a scenario reports user edits or history vanishing after a source refresh, suspect an unstable primary key and prefer moving to a system-of-record identifier with a migration of edits and links.

When a scenario asks what will break if an Ontology resource changes, or which applications use or change an object type, prefer checking Workflow Lineage first over trial changes in production or asking teams informally.

quiz.q: A link from Shipment to Warehouse resolves for most shipments but for none from one source system, whose warehouse ids carry leading zeros that the Warehouse keys lack. What is the right fix?
choices: Change the link to many-to-many so more matches are found
Hide shipments without a warehouse in the module
Give users broader access to the Warehouse object type
Normalize the foreign key to the Warehouse key format in the pipeline and verify that all links resolve
quiz.explain: The evidence points to a key format mismatch, so the fix is normalizing the foreign key and checking resolution; access changes or hiding rows do not address the cause.

quiz.q: Before deleting a link type that looks unused, what should a developer do first?
choices: Check Workflow Lineage for modules, Functions, Actions and automations that use it
Delete it in production and watch for errors
Rename it first and wait to see who complains
Ask in a team chat whether anyone still needs it
quiz.explain: Workflow Lineage lists the actual consumers, so they can be migrated or the link kept; trial-and-error changes break applications and automations unexpectedly.

days.recap: Key objects on stable system-of-record ids, match cardinality and key formats to the data, assemble workflows from Workshop, Actions, Functions and Automate by role, and check Workflow Lineage before changing anything.

days.title: Action Types: Declarative Rules, Function-Backed Actions and Validation

concepts.heading: Actions Are the Governed Write Path
concepts.body: Action types are how users and applications change Ontology objects with validation, permissions and an execution record. There are two implementation styles: declarative edit rules and function-backed Actions. Declarative rules fit direct edits, such as setting an incident's status to Resolved and recording the resolver and time. Do not convert a simple Action to a function-backed one just for future flexibility; convert only when real computation or cascading edits appear. Simpler Actions are easier to review, test and maintain.

concepts.heading: When a Function-Backed Action Is Needed
concepts.body: A function-backed Action fits when the change needs computation (a late fee from days overdue and customer tier), edits to linked objects (incrementing a customer's delivered-orders count), cascades (closing all linked subtasks), or several edits that must succeed or fail together (updating a claim, creating a payment and adjusting coverage). The function returns the edits and the Action applies them together, so there is no half-finished state. Combining an availability check and a reservation in one function-backed Action prevents two users from both booking the last unit. Avoid loading large histories inside an Action, such as every invoice of a customer; update totals incrementally or aggregate server-side instead. Keep tests for the business rules the function encodes.

concepts.heading: Parameters and Forms
concepts.body: Good Actions make bad input hard to submit: required parameters, values chosen from valid lists (such as cost centres), constrained currencies, and dates limited to the future. Default parameters from the user's current selection so forms open pre-filled. For consequential changes, require a reason parameter so the record shows why, alongside the execution history showing who and when. Form-level constraints guide users, but any rule that depends on current object state or on the acting user must also be checked when the Action runs. Treat form constraints as convenience and execution-time checks as the guarantee.

concepts.heading: Submission Criteria Checked at Execution
concepts.body: Submission criteria are evaluated when the Action actually runs, against the current object state and the acting user. Typical criteria: the expense is still in Submitted status, the amount is within the approver's limit, the approver is not the submitter, the target agent is on the same team and not on leave, and no overlapping booking exists for the room. Because objects can change between opening a form and submitting it, these rules cannot live only in the form. Each criterion should carry a specific message naming the failed rule and how to fix it, rather than a generic validation failure. Specific messages reduce support requests and help diagnose rejected submissions.

concepts.heading: Side Effects and Webhooks
concepts.body: Actions can notify external systems through webhooks or side effects tied to a successful submission, for example telling an ERP that a purchase order was approved. External calls must be idempotent, using an idempotency key per submission so a double click or a retry after a timeout does not create duplicates. Failures must be visible and recoverable: record an operation status on the object, alert on errors and allow resending. When the external system may be down, make the internal change first and deliver to the external system asynchronously with retries and visible status. Keep internal multi-object edits atomic and handle external steps with compensation, such as releasing a reservation when a payment fails.

examPoints: When a scenario needs only direct property edits on one object, prefer a declarative Action; when it needs calculations, cascades to linked objects or several edits that must succeed together, prefer a function-backed Action.

When a scenario's rule depends on current object state or on who is acting (self-approval, limits, conflicts), prefer submission criteria evaluated at execution with a clear message over form-only validation or hiding buttons.

quiz.q: An Action must set a Defect's status to Fixed and record who fixed it, and nothing else changes. Which implementation fits?
choices: A function-backed Action, in case the logic grows later
An automation that polls defects and updates them
A declarative Action with edit rules for the two properties
A webhook that asks an external tracker to update the defect
quiz.explain: Direct property edits are exactly what declarative rules are for; function-backed Actions are justified only by computation, cascades or multi-object atomic changes.

quiz.q: Users sometimes double-submit an Action whose webhook creates an entry in a billing system, producing duplicates. Which change addresses the cause?
choices: Remove the webhook and have users create billing entries by hand
Increase the webhook's timeout
Add automatic retries to the webhook without any key
Send an idempotency key per submission so repeated calls create only one entry
quiz.explain: Duplicates come from repeated calls being treated as new ones; an idempotency key makes repeats harmless, while retries without a key make duplicates more likely.

days.recap: Use declarative Actions for direct edits and function-backed Actions for computed, cascading or atomic multi-object changes, enforce state- and user-dependent rules with submission criteria, and make webhooks idempotent and visible.

days.title: Action Security Layers, Testing and Troubleshooting

concepts.heading: Independent Security Layers
concepts.body: Running an Action involves several independent checks: permission to run the Action, permission to edit the target objects, the markings on those objects, and the Action's submission criteria. An Editor role on a project does not imply that every layer passes. Being able to see an object, or even the button, does not grant permission to act on it. Diagnose a denial layer by layer and fix the specific layer that fails. Markings are mandatory and conjunctive, so a user must hold every marking on an object to access it.

concepts.heading: Permission Denials Versus Validation Failures
concepts.body: A permission error means the user lacks one of the security layers, while a validation error means a criterion rejected the inputs or the object's state; each is fixed at its own layer. If an Action fails only for certain objects (executive records, one project, one region), look for object-specific markings or policies that those users lack. If a whole team suddenly loses an Action after a reorganization while nothing changed in the Action, compare their new group membership with the Action's permitted groups. When a marking blocks users, decide with the data owner whether they should handle that data and grant membership through the owner, rather than removing the marking. Never strip a control just to make an error go away.

concepts.heading: Restricting Powerful Actions
concepts.body: Restrict who may run an Action through the Action's own permissions, for example limiting Delete Customer to a data stewardship group; this applies through every application and API, unlike hiding a button. For powerful Actions, also require a reason parameter and review the execution history later. Role-based limits, such as agents issuing credits up to one amount and team leads up to a higher amount, belong in submission criteria, with an approval path for anything above the highest limit. If users complain that validation rejects them, find which rule rejects which submissions and why, then fix wrong rules or unclear messages while keeping protective validation. Removing all validation trades a usability complaint for a data-quality incident.

concepts.heading: Testing Action Changes on Branches
concepts.body: Test changes to an Action on a branch with representative, invalid and edge-case inputs, run as users with and without permission, before review and merge. Include a concurrency case: two submissions on the same object at nearly the same time, checking validation and the final state. Merge an Action together with the Ontology changes it depends on; an Action that references a property existing only on a branch fails for everyone once merged alone. When a property becomes required, update every Action that creates or edits that object type, using lineage to find them. Branch testing protects production objects and users while you verify behaviour.

concepts.heading: Troubleshooting Action Outcomes
concepts.body: If an Action reports success but nothing seems to change, check whether its edit rules target the intended object and property and whether the module refreshes after submission. If an Action succeeds for one object and fails for another from the same form, compare the two objects' state, links, preconditions and permissions. If valid-looking dates fail a rule such as end after start, check conversions such as time zones and date-only versus timestamp values. Intermittent errors saying the object was modified by another user indicate concurrent edits, which call for a clear conflict message and refreshed data. To prove a past execution to an auditor, combine the execution history (user, time, inputs, outcome) with the permissions and criteria in force at that time.

examPoints: When a scenario shows an Action failing for some users or some objects but not others, prefer a layer-by-layer check (Action permission, object edit access, markings, submission criteria) over granting broad roles or removing validation.

When a scenario changes an Action's logic or validation, prefer testing on a branch with valid, invalid, edge, concurrency and permission cases, merged together with any Ontology change it depends on.

quiz.q: A user can view an Order and sees the Cancel button, but submission fails with a permission error on that order only, while other orders work. What should be checked?
choices: Whether the user's browser cache is out of date
Whether the Action should be rewritten as function-backed
Whether that order carries a marking or policy that the user lacks
Whether the module should hide the button for this user
quiz.explain: A failure limited to one object points to an object-level control such as a marking; seeing the button or the object does not prove the user passes every security layer.

quiz.q: An auditor asks who ran an Approve Refund Action last quarter, with which inputs, and under which rules. What evidence fits?
choices: A screenshot of the Action's current configuration
The Action's execution history plus the permissions and criteria in force at that time
The current property values of the refund objects
Written statements from the approvers
quiz.explain: Execution history records who ran the Action, when, with what inputs and outcome; pairing it with the configuration of that time shows the rules that applied, which current values cannot.

days.recap: Action execution passes independent layers (run permission, object access, markings, criteria), so diagnose and fix the failing layer, restrict powerful Actions by permission, and test changes on branches before merging.

days.title: Choosing a Function Paradigm and Querying the Ontology Efficiently

concepts.heading: Three Paradigms: TypeScript v2, Python v2 and AIP Logic
concepts.body: Ontology Functions can be written in TypeScript v2 or Python v2, or built with AIP Logic. The guide asks you to choose by determinism, the need for a language model, required runtime capabilities such as libraries, and who will maintain the code. Deterministic calculations, such as a shipment cost from weight, distance and a tariff table, belong in code. Python fits when the logic needs a Python library and the maintainers work in Python; TypeScript fits when the maintaining team writes TypeScript. If a function's language no longer matches its maintainers, rewrite it with equivalence tests and then switch consumers to the new version.

concepts.heading: AIP Logic for Language Work
concepts.body: AIP Logic is the right tool for interpreting or generating language: classifying free-text maintenance notes, explaining why a claim was flagged, or drafting a polite email from structured reasons. Give it typed inputs and typed outputs, such as an enumeration of ten fault categories, and validate the result. The deterministic rule that follows, such as routing by category, stays in code. Do not use a language model to parse a structured API response or to compute exact amounts; explicit parsing and arithmetic in code are cheaper, testable and exact. Using AI where code suffices adds cost and unpredictability.

concepts.heading: Hybrid Designs and Choosing by Evidence
concepts.body: Many requirements split cleanly: thirty explicit policy rules in code plus an AI check for whether a free-text description fits the claimed damage, or a deterministic churn score plus an AI explanation of its factors. When analysts change rules often, keep the rules deterministic and drive them from a governed rules dataset they can update, using AI only for cases no rule matches. When choosing between a rule-based version and an AI version, weigh measured accuracy, cost per call and the rework caused by errors at real volume. A common good answer is rules first and AI for the remainder. Each part is assigned to the paradigm and maintainers that suit it.

concepts.heading: Server-Side Filters, Aggregations and Ordering
concepts.body: Functions should push work to the server instead of loading objects into memory. To find the top five suppliers by on-time rate over 90 days, filter deliveries server-side and aggregate grouped by supplier, then order and take five. To count overdue shipments per warehouse across millions of objects, filter and aggregate counts grouped by warehouse, returning one row each. For the ten most recent comments on a case, query with server-side ordering by date and a limit of ten. To sum revenue per region, use a sum aggregation rather than loading every Sale object.

concepts.heading: Bounded Traversals, Complete Results and Safe Edits
concepts.body: Multi-hop link traversals such as Customer to Orders to Items to Supplier work in development but time out for large customers in production; bound them with filters, limits and aggregations. Never compute a total from a single page of results; aggregate server-side or iterate every page, and add a test against a known total. When a function edits linked objects, such as closing the open tasks of a cancelled project, select the targets with a server-side filter and return bounded edits, tested on the largest realistic project. A function called from an Action should return all its edits together for the Action to apply in one submission, instead of editing in a loop that can fail halfway. These patterns keep functions fast, correct and consistent.

examPoints: When a scenario's logic is exact, deterministic or audited (fees, tax rules, routing rules), prefer TypeScript v2 or Python v2 chosen by maintainers and libraries; reserve AIP Logic for interpreting or generating language.

When a scenario shows a function timing out or returning low totals on large data, prefer server-side filters, aggregations, ordering with limits and full pagination over loading objects into memory or raising timeouts.

quiz.q: A function must compute a parcel's postage from weight and zone tables, and it will be maintained by developers who write TypeScript. Which paradigm fits?
choices: AIP Logic, so the postage rules can be described in a prompt
A TypeScript v2 function with tests for the table lookups
Python v2, because it is always the faster runtime
An agent with a lookup tool that reads the zone tables
quiz.explain: The logic is deterministic and the maintainers write TypeScript, so a tested TypeScript v2 function fits; a language model adds cost and unpredictability to exact arithmetic.

quiz.q: A function shows each region's revenue by loading every Sale object and summing in code, and it times out for the largest region. What should change?
choices: Increase the function's timeout
Use a server-side sum aggregation grouped by region
Sum only the first page of sales and extrapolate
Split the logic into one copy of the function per region
quiz.explain: Aggregating on the server returns only the totals and scales with data size; longer timeouts or partial pages leave the function slow or wrong.

days.recap: Pick TypeScript v2 or Python v2 for deterministic logic by maintainers and libraries, AIP Logic for language work, and keep functions fast with server-side filters, aggregations, ordering, bounded traversals and complete pagination.

days.title: Function Versioning, Provenance, OSDK Bindings and Testing

concepts.heading: How Function-Backed Actions Apply Edits
concepts.body: In a function-backed Action, the function returns edits and the Action validates and applies them, so the result is still governed by the Action's permissions and submission criteria. The edits are applied together, which avoids partial updates. If such an Action fails with an invalid edit result even though the code compiles and its unit test passes, check the returned edits against the object type's constraints with real inputs: property types, required values and link targets. Hand-made test objects often hide these issues. Testing with real objects on a branch reveals them before users do.

concepts.heading: Versioning and Migrating Consumers
concepts.body: When a function used by several modules and Actions needs a breaking change, such as a new return type, publish a new version, migrate consumers deliberately, and keep the old version until all have moved. Introduce a new parameter as optional with a default so existing callers keep working. Consumers reference specific versions, so a module that still shows old behaviour after a release is probably pinned to the old version and needs its reference updated deliberately. This makes releases predictable: nothing changes for a consumer until its owner moves it. Version discipline is what lets many applications share one function safely.

concepts.heading: OSDK Bindings for External Callers
concepts.body: External applications call published Ontology functions through generated OSDK bindings that reflect the function's types and versions. When a function's signature changes, the external TypeScript application may fail to compile; the right response is to regenerate the OSDK package and update the calls, not to suppress the type errors. Reliable external use depends on published versions, documented return types and regeneration whenever the function changes. When adding an optional parameter, publish the new version and regenerate the OSDK so external callers can adopt it. Type errors after a change are useful signals, not obstacles.

concepts.heading: Provenance and Reproducibility
concepts.body: When a function computes consequential values such as a credit limit, an insurance premium or a shipment ETA, record the function version and the input values used alongside the result. That lets auditors and support staff explain or reproduce any past value. If a function reads a changing external value, such as the current exchange rate, results differ between runs; pass the value in as an explicit input or record the rate and timestamp used. When rules change, for example a rounding rule, publish a new version, keep the old one available and record the version per result. Provenance must be stored when the value is produced; it cannot be reconstructed reliably afterwards.

concepts.heading: Testing and Diagnosing Functions
concepts.body: Protect functions with unit tests on representative and boundary inputs: zero values, maximum discounts, missing tiers, expired promotions, rounding and null properties taken from real data. Before publishing, run the function on a branch against real objects, including the largest realistic volumes for bulk edits, then publish a version. When a bug appears, first add a test with the failing input, then fix the logic and verify against known results. If a user-scoped function returns an empty list or an object type not found error only for some users, check those users' access to the data before changing code, because queries run with their permissions. Handle missing or invisible linked objects explicitly, and use execution traces and timings to find which steps are slow for which inputs.

examPoints: When a scenario changes a function used by modules, Actions or OSDK applications, prefer publishing a new version (with new parameters optional and defaulted), migrating consumers deliberately and regenerating the OSDK over editing in place.

When a scenario shows a user-scoped function returning less data or a not-found error only for some users, prefer checking those users' access to the underlying data before changing code or execution mode.

quiz.q: Regulators require that any past discount computed by a function can be explained later. What should be stored with each discount?
choices: Only the final discount amount
The function version and the input values used to compute it
A screenshot of the module at the time of calculation
The name of the developer who last edited the function
quiz.explain: Version plus inputs is what makes a result reproducible and explainable; the amount alone cannot show which logic or data produced it.

quiz.q: After a function's return type changed in a new version, an external TypeScript application calling it no longer compiles. What should the developer do?
choices: Regenerate the OSDK package and update the application's calls to match
Cast the result to an untyped value to silence the errors
Roll back the Ontology so the old type returns
Copy the function's code into the application
quiz.explain: Generated OSDK bindings reflect the function's published types, so regenerating and updating calls is the supported path; suppressing types hides real breakage.

days.recap: Publish function changes as versions and migrate consumers deliberately, regenerate OSDK bindings for external callers, record version and inputs with consequential results, and test with real, edge-case data on branches.

days.title: Workshop Building Blocks: Pages, Widgets, Variables and Ontology Connections

concepts.heading: Variables Connect Widgets
concepts.body: Workshop modules are built from pages, sections and widgets that pass information through variables. A table's selected-object output variable can feed a details panel, so the panel always shows what the user picked. Shared filter variables applied to one object set variable can drive both a chart and a table, so they always reflect the same filters. Selections can be chained: a map selection sets a site variable, which filters an asset list, whose selection becomes an Action parameter for creating a work order. Thinking in variables rather than separate queries per widget keeps the module consistent.

concepts.heading: Pages, Sections and Conditional Visibility
concepts.body: Organize a module around the workflow's steps, for example search, review and decide, using pages or sections with clear navigation and passing the selected object between them as a variable. Conditional visibility shows elements only in certain states, such as an approval panel for pending requests or a warning banner driven by a derived boolean variable. Visibility is a usability feature, not security, so the same rule must also be enforced by the Action's submission criteria. If a conditional section never appears, check the variable used and the exact compared value, such as case or a code versus its display label. For large value sets, such as hundreds of regions, use a searchable filter that supports all values.

concepts.heading: Showing Ontology Data and Writing Through Actions
concepts.body: Display Ontology data through object tables and other widgets bound to object sets, for example the selected customer's linked open tickets. Change object state through Action buttons or inline Actions, which run the configured Action type with its validation and permissions. Bind Action parameters to selection variables so forms open pre-filled; an empty form usually means the defaults are not bound. A review queue is a table of pending items, a details panel bound to the selection, and Approve and Reject Actions with a reason. After an Action, refresh the views that show the changed objects.

concepts.heading: Functions and Computed Values
concepts.body: Function-backed variables and function-backed columns show computed values, such as a risk score for the selected customer or a workload score for each of a manager's direct reports. When a value is used to sort or filter thousands of rows and changes only daily, materialize it as a property through a pipeline instead of computing it per row, and compute exact live values only for the selected item. Rarely changing aggregates over millions of objects should likewise be stored rather than recomputed on every load. External data, such as a weather or currency feed, should reach the module through the platform, for example a Function, rather than being called directly from the page, which exposes the call to the client and repeats it on every load. The page should read governed data from the Ontology.

concepts.heading: Integrating AI in Workshop
concepts.body: On-demand AI features, such as a case summary or a next-best-action suggestion that takes several seconds, should run when the user asks: a button calls an AIP Logic function for the selected object and shows a typed result with loading and error states. If colleagues need to see the output later, persist it through a function-backed Action that stores the summary with its author and time. Display AI answers with citations linking to the objects they used, so users can verify them. Avoid generating AI output on every page load when users only sometimes need it. Optionally store results for reuse to save time and cost.

examPoints: When a scenario needs widgets to react to a user's selection or filters, prefer variables (selection outputs, shared filter variables and one object set) feeding both widgets and Action parameters over separate queries per widget.

When a scenario needs a computed value to sort or filter thousands of rows, prefer a materialized property and compute live values only for the selected item; when AI output is needed only sometimes, prefer an on-demand function call with loading and error states.

quiz.q: A module lists work orders and should show the selected order's details beside the list. Where should the details widgets get their object?
choices: From a separate search box where the user types the order id again
From a hard-coded object id configured in the panel
From a reload of the page with the id added to the address
From the list's selected-object output variable
quiz.explain: Selection output variables are how Workshop widgets pass context to each other, keeping the panel in step with the list without extra user steps.

quiz.q: An Escalate button should appear only for open cases older than 72 hours. Which design is sound?
choices: Conditional visibility alone, since a hidden button cannot be used
Conditional visibility from a derived variable, with the Action's submission criteria enforcing the same rule
Showing the button to everyone and relying on users' judgement
A separate module for each age group of cases
quiz.explain: Visibility improves the interface, but only submission criteria guarantee the rule wherever the Action is invoked, so both are combined.

days.recap: Wire Workshop widgets through variables, organize pages by workflow step, write through Actions with pre-filled parameters, materialize values used for sorting, and run occasional AI on demand with clear states and citations.

days.title: Workshop Performance, Deployment and Module Interfaces

concepts.heading: Variable Dependencies Drive Recomputation
concepts.body: Every variable recomputes when something it depends on changes, so unnecessary dependencies make modules slow. An expensive function-backed variable that depends on unrelated filters recomputes on every filter change; make it depend only on the inputs it uses. A chart that depends on the table's row selection recomputes on every click; it should depend only on the filter. If three variables update one after another and each triggers a chart, consolidate them into one combined variable that updates once. A heavy aggregation should depend on its data inputs, not on navigation state such as which tab is open.

concepts.heading: Lazy Loading and Sensible Defaults
concepts.body: The guide lists lazy loading and performance refactoring among Workshop skills. Content in hidden tabs or collapsed sections, and the variables behind it, should load only when opened. Default a large table to the subset users need, such as today's items, with pagination and derived columns computed only for visible rows. Share one base object set across widgets instead of letting each widget run its own heavy query, and move rarely used charts or maps to tabs loaded on demand. Hiding slowness behind a spinner does not remove it, which the guide warns against.

concepts.heading: Asynchronous Events and Stale Views
concepts.body: Workshop updates are asynchronous, so the order of updates matters. When a table still shows old values after an Action, refresh the dependent widgets from the Action's completion event rather than adding fixed delays. If a table reads a chart's selection and sometimes shows data for the previous filter, the selection is stale; reset it or derive it from the filter. When an Action is followed by a long calculation that freezes the page, move the calculation to a background automation and show its status in the module. Diagnose stale views through variable dependencies and update order before redesigning.

concepts.heading: Embedded Module Interfaces Are Contracts
concepts.body: A module embedded in other modules exposes input and output variables, and parent modules depend on them. Renaming an output, adding a required input or changing a default value can break parents owned by other teams. Compatible changes are additive: a new optional input whose default preserves current behaviour, or a new list input added alongside an existing single-object input. Before changing a default, find parents through lineage and set the value explicitly where they rely on it. Repeated interface pieces, such as a customer header built five times, are best factored into one reusable embedded module with a stable input.

concepts.heading: Deployment Channels and Audiences
concepts.body: Different audiences can get different layouts over the same logic: tablet pages with large controls for field staff and dense tables for managers, all sharing the same Actions and Functions. Use one module with conditional sections when differences are small, and audience-specific modules over shared components when they diverge a lot. Partners can get a dedicated module showing only partner pages and Actions, backed by data-level permissions, or a scoped OSDK portal sharing the same Ontology logic. Substantial redesigns and heavy new pages should be built and tuned on a branch or new version, piloted with a small group, then released with monitoring and a rollback option. This avoids disrupting hundreds of daily users.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a slow module, prefer lazy loading hidden content, trimming variable dependencies, sharing a base object set and defaulting to a filtered, paginated subset over adding a spinner or splitting the module into copies.

When a scenario changes an embedded module used by other teams, prefer additive, optional inputs with behaviour-preserving defaults and lineage-driven migration of parents over renaming variables or making inputs required.

quiz.q: An embedded module is used by four parent modules, and its owner wants to support a new filter. Which change is backward compatible?
choices: Adding an optional input whose default keeps the current behaviour
Renaming the existing input to match the new design
Adding the new input as required so parents must set it
Changing an existing input's default without telling the parents
quiz.explain: Additive, optional inputs with behaviour-preserving defaults leave existing parents working; renames, required inputs and silent default changes break the interface contract.

quiz.q: A module's table shows old values right after an Action succeeds, until users reload the page. What is the best fix?
choices: Refresh the table from the Action's completion event
Add a fixed five-second wait before the table reads data
Ask users to reload the page after each submission
Replace the Action with an automation
quiz.explain: Refreshing on the completion event updates the view exactly when the write is done; fixed delays are unreliable and manual reloads are a workaround, not a fix.

days.recap: Keep Workshop fast with tight variable dependencies, lazy loading and filtered defaults, refresh from Action completion events, treat embedded module interfaces as contracts, and release large changes through branches and pilots.

days.title: Workshop or OSDK, Application Registration and Authentication

concepts.heading: Choosing Workshop, OSDK or a Hybrid
concepts.body: The guide asks you to choose Workshop, the OSDK or a hybrid and justify the choice. Prefer Workshop for internal workflows made of forms, tables and charts, especially for teams with little front-end experience, because it meets the need with less code. Choose the OSDK for customer-facing portals with custom branding, tailored mobile experiences, users without Foundry accounts, or embedding Foundry data and Actions inside an existing application. A hybrid shares Actions and Functions, with a Workshop module for internal staff and a scoped OSDK portal for partners. The audience and the security model usually decide the answer.

concepts.heading: Registration, Scopes and OSDK Generation
concepts.body: An external application is registered with an authentication flow, scopes and redirect URLs, and the OSDK package is generated for that scope. Scopes should list exactly the object types and Actions the application uses, such as reads of Product and Order and one Create Return Request Action. Redirect URLs should be registered exactly for each environment. When a new feature needs another object type or Action, add it to the scope and regenerate the OSDK; otherwise the build fails or calls return scope errors even for users who can use that resource elsewhere. Putting scope review and regeneration into the release checklist and CI prevents these surprises.

concepts.heading: User-Based Authentication
concepts.body: User-based OAuth suits applications that people sign in to: each call runs under the signed-in user's identity, so results reflect that user's permissions and changes are attributed to individuals in audit records. Effective access is the intersection of the application's scope and the user's permissions, so a user who can run an Action in Workshop still cannot run it through an app whose scope lacks it. An internal application that uses one service identity for everyone shows everyone all data and makes audit attribution impossible; switching to user-based OAuth fixes both. When only one organization's users fail after signing in, check whether the application is enabled for that organization and whether those users may access its resources. Use this flow whenever results or audit must reflect individuals.

concepts.heading: Service-Based Authentication
concepts.body: Service-based authentication with client credentials suits headless work with no user present, such as a nightly sync to an ERP or a partner server reading a curated set of objects. Give each job or portal its own client with the minimum scope it needs, and keep the secret on the server. A public portal for customers without Foundry accounts uses a backend with a scoped service client that authenticates customers itself and returns only each customer's own data. Restrict what the credential can read at the data level, for example to one partner's orders, with filtering in integration code only as a second layer. An application can combine both flows: user-based for its screens and service-based for its background job.

concepts.heading: Keeping Secrets Safe
concepts.body: The guide asks you to choose authentication without exposing secrets. A client secret placed in front-end code is visible to anyone who opens the page; the fix is to rotate it, move secret-based calls to a server (or use user-based OAuth for interactive use), and minimize the scope. A long-lived secret that was sent by email and never rotated should be replaced: issue a new scoped credential through a secure channel, migrate the partner, then revoke the old secret. Credentials must never be pasted into code repositories, chats or documents. Least privilege applies to both the scope of the application and the access of its service identity.

examPoints: When a scenario has employees signing in and needs per-user permissions or individual attribution, prefer user-based OAuth; when no user is present (nightly jobs, partner servers), prefer a separate, minimally scoped service client with its secret kept server-side.

When a scenario shows an OSDK application failing on a resource that the user can use in Workshop, prefer adding that resource to the application's scope and regenerating the OSDK over granting the user more permissions.

quiz.q: An hourly background job syncs statuses to an external system with nobody signed in. How should it authenticate?
choices: A developer's personal OAuth token stored in the job's configuration
A service secret embedded in the application's front-end code
An administrator account shared by the whole team
A service client scoped to the needed resources, with its secret held on the server
quiz.explain: Headless work calls for service-based authentication with minimal scope and a server-side secret; personal tokens, shared admin accounts and exposed secrets break least privilege and accountability.

quiz.q: An internal approval tool for 150 employees needs forms and tables, and the team has little front-end experience. What should they consider first?
choices: A custom React application, because the OSDK is always more flexible
A public portal using service-based authentication
Exporting the data to spreadsheets for approvals
Whether Workshop meets the need before building a custom OSDK application
quiz.explain: For internal, standard forms-and-tables needs Workshop delivers with less code; the OSDK is chosen when custom experiences or external audiences require it.

days.recap: Prefer Workshop for internal standard UIs and the OSDK for custom or external ones, scope applications to exactly what they use, use user-based OAuth for people and minimally scoped server-side service clients for headless work.

days.title: Reading, Aggregating and Writing Through the OSDK and REST APIs, and Diagnosing Failures

concepts.heading: Aggregations Instead of Client-Side Sums
concepts.body: When an external application needs totals or counts, such as contract value per region across millions of objects, use an OSDK aggregation that groups and sums on the platform and returns only the totals. For per-entity counts, such as open tickets for each of 2,000 customers, one grouped aggregation request replaces thousands of individual calls. Dashboards refreshed frequently should use grouped aggregations on a sensible interval, with caching. If an external report's totals differ from Workshop for the same filters, the app is probably missing pages or filtering differently; use the same server-side aggregation and filters. Fetching objects to sum them client-side is slow, costly and error-prone.

concepts.heading: Pagination and Page Tokens
concepts.body: Large object lists must be fetched page by page with server-side ordering, for example 50 suppliers at a time sorted by name, using the page token returned with each page to request the next. A tool that lists recently modified records and sometimes misses some is a classic sign of reading only the first page. The fix is to follow page tokens until none remain on every call. This applies equally to the OSDK and to REST API calls. Only load what the user is viewing, and never assume one page holds the whole result.

concepts.heading: Writing Through Actions
concepts.body: External applications should change Ontology state by invoking Actions through the OSDK, so the same validation, permissions and audit apply as in Workshop. An operation that must succeed as a whole, such as creating a ticket with its required customer link, should be a single Action call with the link as a required parameter. A delivery app can pass a photo as an Action parameter and let the Action validate the driver's assignment and the delivery's status. Offline apps can queue the intended Action calls and replay them on reconnection, handling validation failures and conflicts per call. When an Action rejects a call, show the user its specific validation message rather than a generic error.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Authentication and Scope Failures
concepts.body: If an app can read objects but fails on an Action the user can run in Workshop, the application's scope lacks that Action. If a teammate narrowed the scopes, resources removed from scope fail for every user regardless of their permissions. If users land on an error page right after login following a deployment or a domain move, register the new redirect URL. If calls fail with authorization errors about an hour after sign-in and work after signing in again, the app is not refreshing expired tokens. When development works and production returns empty results, compare the two registrations' scopes, enabled resources and target environments.

concepts.heading: Resilience, Rate Limits and Ontology Change
concepts.body: Rate-limit errors at peak hours call for less traffic (batching, aggregations, caching stable data) plus exponential backoff with jitter, and bulk jobs that call an Action per object should also make those calls idempotent. Apps should use timeouts with clear errors and visible status for writes instead of an endless spinner. When the Ontology changes, such as a renamed property, regenerate the OSDK and update the code; after upgrading the package, review the generated type changes. Pin OSDK package versions, track Ontology changes, and regenerate and test deliberately on a branch. Log errors by category (expired credentials, scope errors, rate limits) and alert the owners before users report problems.

examPoints: When a scenario needs totals or counts over many objects from an external application, prefer a server-side grouped aggregation over fetching pages and summing client-side; when it lists many objects, prefer server-ordered pagination that follows page tokens to the end.

When a scenario shows sign-in or call failures after a deployment or change, prefer finding the specific cause (redirect URL, token refresh, application scope, rate limits) and fixing it narrowly over broadening permissions or disabling checks.

quiz.q: An external app's users are sent to an error page right after login, but only since the app moved to a new domain. What is the likely fix?
choices: Grant the users additional Ontology roles
Register the new domain's redirect URL for the application
Regenerate the OSDK package
Switch the application to service-based authentication
quiz.explain: A failure immediately after login that began with a domain move points to an unregistered redirect URL; roles and SDK bindings are unrelated to the sign-in redirect.

quiz.q: An external app must let drivers mark deliveries complete, with validation that the driver is assigned. How should it write the change?
choices: Invoke a Complete Delivery Action through the OSDK and let the Action validate
Write directly to the backing dataset from the app
Check the assignment in the app, then update the property without an Action
Email the dispatcher so they can update the record
quiz.explain: Actions apply the same validation, permissions and audit for every caller, so external apps should change state through them rather than bypassing governance.

days.recap: From external apps, aggregate on the server, follow page tokens to the end, write through Actions, diagnose auth failures by their specific cause, and handle rate limits and Ontology changes with backoff, pinning and regeneration.

days.title: Automate: Triggers, Conditions, Effects, Retries and Ownership

concepts.heading: Event Triggers Versus Schedules
concepts.body: The guide asks you to select triggers and evaluation modes that fit the requirement. Event triggers suit immediate reactions to changes, such as notifying on-call staff when an incident's severity is raised to Critical or running a credit check when a high-value order is created. Schedules suit periodic work, such as a Monday summary of overdue tasks, a nightly job closing old drafts, or a daily reminder about contracts expiring in 30 days. An automation that polls 200,000 objects every five minutes to spot changes is expensive and late; replace it with an event trigger on the specific change. Many requirements combine both: immediate alerts for critical items and a daily digest for the rest.

concepts.heading: Conditions Decide Whether, Effects Decide What
concepts.body: Conditions decide whether an automation acts at all, for example only for orders above a value; effects describe what it does. A threshold crossing is a transition, not a state: to fire once when a temperature passes 90 degrees, condition on the change from at or below 90 to above 90, not on the value being above 90. For a status change, use a property-change trigger with a condition on the new value. Conditions must compare against the exact stored values, since a code and its display label can differ. Keeping the decision in conditions makes automations easier to read and test.

concepts.heading: Whose Permissions Effects Use
concepts.body: According to the Automate documentation, condition evaluation and Action and Logic effects run with the permissions of the automation's owner in every scoping mode, while notification effects use each recipient's permissions. Saving an automation can transfer ownership to the person who saved it, and an automation owned by a third-party application runs as that application's service user. Project scope changes who can see the run history and requires the resources to be imported into the project; it does not change whose permissions are used. To limit what an automation can read or change, give it a least-privilege owner, such as a scoped service user. Knowing this explains why an automation can act on objects the triggering user cannot see.

concepts.heading: Retries, Backoff and Fallbacks
concepts.body: Retries can be configured on Action and Logic effects, and fallback effects exist for when an effect still fails. Use a bounded number of retries with backoff and jitter rather than many immediate retries that hammer a failing system and flood logs. For long external outages, a fallback can mark the work as pending for later replay and alert the owning team. For rate-limited external APIs, limit concurrency, back off on rate-limit errors and batch where possible. The order of multiple Action effects in one automation is not guaranteed, so do not design steps that rely on it.

concepts.heading: Ownership and Actionable Notifications
concepts.body: Automations should be owned by a team, not an individual, with failures routed to a team channel or on-call rotation; otherwise failures silently go to someone who changed roles or left. Review ownership periodically, and when a team moves its alerts to a new channel, update the destination and send a test. An orphaned automation that nobody understands should be investigated with lineage and its run history, then adopted by a team or retired. Too many low-value alerts get ignored, so send only actionable failures to the team and put warnings in a digest. Tuning conditions often removes the noise at its source.

examPoints: When a scenario needs an immediate reaction to a specific change, prefer an event trigger with a condition (a transition for threshold crossings); when it needs periodic summaries or cleanup, prefer a schedule with a bounded query.

When a scenario asks whose permissions an automation's Action or Logic effects use, remember that they run as the automation's owner in every scoping mode, and prefer a least-privilege, team-controlled owner such as a scoped service user over a personal account.

quiz.q: An automation should alert when a tank's pressure rises above a limit, but not keep alerting while it stays high. Which configuration fits?
choices: A condition that the pressure is above the limit, checked on every update
A schedule every minute that alerts on all tanks above the limit
A condition on the transition from at or below the limit to above it
An Action that operators run when they notice high pressure
quiz.explain: A transition condition fires once per crossing; a state condition or a frequent schedule repeats the alert for as long as the value stays high.

quiz.q: An automation is moved into a project scope, and a reviewer asks whether its Action effects now use project permissions. What is correct?
choices: Yes: project scope makes effects run with the project's combined permissions
Effects switch to the permissions of the user whose change triggered the run
No: Action and Logic effects still run as the automation's owner; scope changes run-history visibility
Effects run without any permissions until the project is approved
quiz.explain: The Automate documentation states that Action and Logic effects use the owner's permissions in every scoping mode; project scope affects history visibility and requires imported resources.

days.recap: Use event triggers for immediate reactions and schedules for periodic work, put the decision in conditions, remember effects run as the owner, and configure bounded retries, fallbacks and team ownership with actionable alerts.

days.title: At-Least-Once Execution, Races, Live Changes and Testing Automations

concepts.heading: At-Least-Once Execution Means Duplicates
concepts.body: The guide asks you to account for at-least-once execution: an automation can run more than once for the same event, events can be redelivered after a platform hiccup, and two near-simultaneous updates can each meet the condition. Effects must therefore be idempotent, so running them twice has the same result as running them once. Common techniques are a per-object idempotency key, checking a notified flag or an existing follow-up task before creating one, and deterministic keys for created objects. Notifications can be keyed on the object and its new status, so a duplicate for the same change is skipped. Disabling retries does not solve duplicates and makes failures worse.

concepts.heading: Partial Failures With External Systems
concepts.body: External calls can succeed on the other side while the automation sees a timeout, for example an ERP that accepts an invoice but whose response is lost, so a retry would create a second invoice. Send an idempotency key per invoice or contract, record the external reference once the call is confirmed, and look up existing status before creating anything on retry. Recording status after success also covers the case where the invoice was created but the status was never written. Make external effects idempotent before relying on retries. Reconciliation then has the data it needs.

concepts.heading: Races and Live State
concepts.body: Independent automations reacting to the same update can race: a total may be computed before a discount is applied, or a survey may link to attachments that another automation has not finished archiving. Fix this by chaining dependent steps or combining them into one ordered workflow, not by hoping one finishes first. Users also change their minds: an invoice approved and then rejected a minute later, or an order marked Shipped by mistake. Re-check the current state just before an external effect, and design a correction or reversal path in case something was already sent. For short-lived changes, such as brief customer segment moves, debounce and re-check before sending communications.

concepts.heading: Changing Live Automations
concepts.body: Changing a live automation affects runs that are in progress or queued, so treat it as a planned change. Understand what is in flight, test the change first, apply it at a quiet time or between scheduled runs, and monitor afterwards. When rules change, such as customer tier rules in a nightly job, record the rule version applied to each object so results can be explained later. The guide asks you to account for live changes and in-flight work. Unplanned edits to busy automations are a common source of inconsistent results.

concepts.heading: Testing and Diagnosing Automations
concepts.body: Test new automations with representative objects and safe effects, such as a test recipient, or run them manually on test objects and review the effects before enabling live triggers. Enable critical or large automations in stages for a small monitored segment, keeping a quick way to stop them (such as muting) and a rollback plan. When an automation goes silent, check whether it is muted and read the evaluation and effect history to see whether conditions matched and whether effects ran or were skipped. Conditions that evaluate but never match usually compare against the wrong stored value; skipped effects point to mute state, the owner's permissions or effect conditions. If an Action effect fails with submission criteria not met, align the automation's condition with the Action's criteria, and if an effect succeeds but no object appears, trace the Action's execution record for that run.

examPoints: When a scenario reports duplicate notices, tasks or invoices from an automation, prefer idempotent effects (a per-object key, an existence check or a recorded external reference) over disabling retries or hoping events arrive once.

When a scenario shows an automation's condition matching but its effect rejected or silently skipped, prefer evidence from evaluation and effect history (mute state, owner permissions, Action criteria) over rewriting or recreating the automation.

quiz.q: An automation that books a courier when an order is packed occasionally books two couriers for one order after events were redelivered. What is the right fix?
choices: Use a per-order idempotency key and record the booking reference so repeats are skipped
Turn off retries on the effect
Add a weekly automation that cancels duplicate bookings
Ask the courier company to ignore duplicates by hand
quiz.explain: Because execution is at least once, the effect itself must be idempotent; turning off retries loses real failures and cleanup jobs act after the damage is done.

quiz.q: An automation's history shows conditions matching, but its Action effect fails with submission criteria not met. What does this indicate?
choices: The automation is muted
The Action's criteria reject the change at execution, so the automation's condition should be aligned with them
The trigger never fired
The effect needs more retries
quiz.explain: The history shows the trigger fired and the condition matched, so the rejection happens at the Action's own validation layer; retries would fail the same way.

days.recap: Design automation effects for at-least-once execution with idempotency keys and recorded references, order dependent steps and re-check live state, change live automations deliberately, and diagnose from evaluation and effect history.

days.title: Where AI Adds Value: AIP Logic, Agents and Minimum Capability

concepts.heading: Use AI Where Interpretation Is Needed
concepts.body: The guide asks when AI adds value over deterministic logic. AI fits interpreting unstructured content: classifying free-text feedback into themes, extracting the complaint and requested remedy from a letter, or drafting a reply that references a customer's open orders. Rules, validations, exact calculations and authorization stay deterministic. A good AI feature does the interpretation and hands a typed result to deterministic code or to a person. Choosing AI for arithmetic or permission checks is a common distractor.

concepts.heading: Typed Inputs and Outputs
concepts.body: AIP Logic functions should take typed inputs, such as an incident description and its linked asset, and return typed outputs. Categories and priorities become enumerations (for example P1 to P4) with a short reason; extractions become structs, such as vendor, numeric amount, currency and due date, plus a confidence or quoted evidence field. Validate the output before using it, for example converting an amount written in words into a number. Typed outputs can pre-fill an Action form that a person confirms. For routing, a confidence value lets uncertain items go to a triage queue instead of being auto-routed.

concepts.heading: Logic Functions, Agents and Grounded Answers
concepts.body: Use a Logic function or code for a fixed task with defined inputs and outputs, and an agent for open-ended, multi-turn work, such as a chat panel where engineers investigate an incident and the agent looks up related records with scoped tools. When answers must come from documents, such as HR policies, retrieve the relevant chunks from the Ontology, instruct the model to answer only from them, and return citations to the source sections in a typed output. Citations let users verify answers and make errors traceable. Store AI suggestions separately from human-confirmed values.

concepts.heading: Minimum Data and Capabilities
concepts.body: Give an AI feature only the data and tools its task requires. A case summary needs the case and its linked objects with read-only access, not every object type and every Action. Pass only the needed fields: a renewal email needs name, open tickets and tier, not payment details or internal risk notes. If an assistant leaks salary figures because a tool returns full employee records, narrow the tool instead of adding a prompt instruction, and remove write tools the task does not need. Retrieve context with the requesting user's permissions rather than a broad service identity, so users never receive data they could not otherwise see.

concepts.heading: Keep People in Control of Consequential Changes
concepts.body: Let AI prepare consequential changes, such as a refund, a discount or a cancellation, and require the user to confirm them through a validated Action whose submission criteria enforce limits. If a user tricks an agent into cancelling other customers' orders by pasting instructions into a comment, the defence is a tool scoped to the order in context, the user's own permissions, validation and confirmation, not a stricter prompt. Bounded autonomy is acceptable when limits are enforced in the Action, for example automatic refunds capped at a small amount. Cache AI results by input version and regenerate only when inputs change, to control cost. The guide asks you to prevent unsafe actions, not to trust the model's judgement.

examPoints: When a scenario lets an AI feature change data (cancel, refund, discount), prefer having the AI prepare the change for user confirmation through a validated Action whose criteria enforce limits over relying on prompt instructions.

When a scenario shows an AI feature exposing data it should not, prefer narrowing its inputs and tools and retrieving as the requesting user over adding instructions to the prompt or switching models.

quiz.q: A support team is planning several features. Which one is the clearest fit for AIP Logic rather than deterministic code?
choices: Calculating a late fee from days overdue and a rate table
Tagging free-text product reviews with one of eight complaint themes
Blocking requesters from approving their own expense claims
Checking whether a user belongs to the group allowed to run an Action
quiz.explain: Interpreting unstructured text is where AI adds value; fee calculations, validation rules and authorization should stay deterministic and governed.

quiz.q: A help-desk agent answers employees' questions about their own IT tickets. One of its tools can close tickets, which the feature never needs. What should the developer do?
choices: Remove the ticket-closing tool and keep read-only tools limited to the asking employee's tickets
Keep the tool and add a prompt rule never to close tickets
Keep the tool and review a log of its use each month
Run the agent under a service identity that can read every ticket
quiz.explain: Minimum capability means removing tools the task does not need and reading as the requesting user; prompt rules and logs do not prevent misuse of a write tool, and a broad identity widens exposure.

days.recap: Use AI for interpretation with typed, validated outputs, agents for open-ended work, give AI only the data and tools it needs under the user's permissions, and keep consequential changes behind confirmed, validated Actions.

days.title: Evaluating AI Features and Reviewing AI FDE-Generated Code

concepts.heading: Evaluation Suites
concepts.body: Before releasing or changing an AI feature, build an evaluation suite of representative and edge cases with expected outputs; for an AI-backed Action proposing refund amounts, include checks that proposals respect policy limits. Keep the suite representative of real inputs: if users report poor summaries for very long cases and the suite holds mostly short ones, add long cases. When inputs drift, such as a new product category the prompt does not mention, update the prompt's categories and examples and add cases for the new category. Compare prompt versions on the same suite with repeated runs and per-category results before keeping or reverting a change. Evaluation turns opinions about quality into evidence.

concepts.heading: Traces for Diagnosis
concepts.body: Traces show what each run actually received and produced, which is the first place to look when output is wrong. If a summary states facts not in the case, check whether those facts were in the context, then constrain the prompt and add grounding cases. If a prompt has grown to tens of thousands of tokens because every linked document is injected in full, trim to relevant documents and summaries and compare quality, latency and cost. If more context doubled latency for a one-point accuracy gain, use traces to keep only the context that measurably helps. More context is not automatically better.

concepts.heading: Production Feedback and Cost
concepts.body: In production, record each run linked to the user's accept, edit or reject decision and their corrections, so you know how often suggestions help and where they fail. Link thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback to traces, review the negatives, and turn verified failures into evaluation cases and targeted fixes. When costs jump, examine usage and traces per feature: call counts, tokens per call and the sources of growth. If unchanged documents are summarized many times a day, cache summaries by document version with permission-aware access and regenerate only when the document changes. Monitoring quality and cost together keeps AI features sustainable.

concepts.heading: Reviewing AI FDE-Generated Functions
concepts.body: The guide asks developers to review Function code generated by AI FDE for schema, platform idioms, provenance and side-effect safety before publishing. Check the code against the actual Ontology schema and generated types, since generated code can reference an object type that does not exist under that name. Check platform idioms: bounded, server-side filtered queries with pagination instead of loading every object, edits through the governed mechanism, and typed query APIs with parameters instead of filters built by concatenating user text. Code that compiles and passes a quick manual test can still violate all of these. AI FDE works in the user's own session and needs user consent for writes, which does not replace review of what the code does.

concepts.heading: Side-Effect Safety and Review Process
concepts.body: Side effects need the closest review. Separate recommending from applying, so a generated function that recommends a discount does not also apply it outside a governed Action. Creation and external calls must be idempotent so retries after a timeout do not duplicate tasks or emails, and status updates should follow a confirmed send. Add edit-scope checks and tests asserting exactly which objects are edited, since a missing project filter can edit objects outside the intended scope. Keep a mandatory, lightweight human review for every generated function, even small ones, and automate the mechanical checks with tests and a branch run.

examPoints: When a scenario questions an AI feature's quality or suspects a prompt change caused a regression, prefer running an evaluation suite on both versions together with traces of real runs over switching to a bigger model or adding more context.

When a scenario involves Function code generated by AI FDE, prefer a mandatory review of schema match, platform idioms, provenance and side-effect safety, with tests and a branch run, over publishing because the code compiles and passes a quick test.

quiz.q: An AI-drafted incident report names a root cause that engineers say appears nowhere in the incident's records. What is the best first step?
choices: Move the feature to a larger model
Add every linked document to the prompt in full
Skip the evaluation suite for the next release to ship a fix faster
Read the run's trace to see whether that cause was in the context the model received
quiz.explain: Traces show whether the problem is the context or the generation, which decides the fix; bigger models and more context are guesses that add cost and latency.

quiz.q: An AI FDE-generated function creates a follow-up task for each overdue invoice, and its caller retries after timeouts. Nothing stops the same task from being created twice. What should the reviewer require?
choices: Idempotent creation, such as a deterministic key or an existence check, with a test for a repeated call
Publishing it as is, since it compiled and passed a quick test
Turning off retries in the caller so that duplicates cannot occur
Running it under an administrator identity so duplicates can be cleaned up later
quiz.explain: Retries after a timeout are normal, so creation must be idempotent and tested for repeats; disabling retries loses real failures, and broad identities do not prevent duplicates.

days.recap: Prove AI quality with representative evaluation suites, diagnose with traces and production feedback, control cost with caching by input version, and review every AI FDE-generated function for schema, idioms, provenance and side effects.

days.title: Data Controls, Branch Protection and Application Versus Data Access

concepts.heading: The Layers of Control
concepts.body: Application security combines several controls: roles on projects for resource access, organizations, markings, restricted views, object and property security policies, Action permissions and branch protection.
