Markings are mandatory and conjunctive and propagate through transform and analysis logic, so derived data stays protected. Restricted views are built on a backing dataset, filter rows only and cannot be used as an input for transforms. Object and property security policies give row-, column- and cell-level control in the Ontology and are recommended over restricted views for most Ontology use cases. The guide asks you to apply least privilege and governance controls rather than rely on application code.

concepts.heading: Row- and Property-Level Protection
concepts.body: Visibility rules belong in the data layer, not in application filters or hidden columns. Regional row visibility, such as adjusters seeing only their region's claims while supervisors see all, is an object security policy (or a restricted view backing the type) keyed on a region attribute. A sensitive property such as salary or a performance rating needs property-level control, possibly attribute-based so a manager sees only their reports' ratings, or a separate restricted object type. Several roles can be served from one dataset by combining row policies (by clinic) and property controls (clinical notes for clinicians only). Hiding a column in one module leaves the data readable through every other path.

concepts.heading: Application Access Versus Data Access
concepts.body: The guide asks you to separate application access from data access. Being able to open an application depends on access to the application resource, such as a role on its project or folder, and on being in the group it was shared with. Seeing data inside it depends on access to the object types and backing data each page or section reads. So a user who cannot open the app needs resource sharing checked, while a user whose tables are empty, or whose single column is blank, needs the exact data permission or property-level control checked. Share a module broadly and let each user's data permissions decide what they see within it, including who sees financial figures.

concepts.heading: Least Privilege When Fixing Access
concepts.body: When a user hits an access error, identify the exact failing permission and change only that; granting Owner on every project the application touches is the classic wrong answer. Contractors should get time-bound access through a dedicated group with application access and only the data their tasks need. An external auditor can get a read-only module with data limited to the needed objects and access that expires. Partner organizations can share a module with data-level controls limiting them to partner objects. After a reorganization with mixed symptoms, triage by symptom, trace dependencies with lineage and fix each exact control.

concepts.heading: Branch Protection for Production Changes
concepts.body: Branch protection requiring an approving review before merging to production ensures that changes to Actions and Functions are reviewed. It prevents incidents such as a validation rule being removed by a direct, unreviewed merge, after which invalid data enters the Ontology. If that has already happened, restore the rule, correct the invalid records and then enable protection. Teams that worry about speed can keep reviews fast with small changes and quick branch builds rather than dropping review. Review is a governance control, like markings, not optional process.

examPoints: When a scenario requires that some users see only some rows or properties, prefer data-level controls (object or property security policies, restricted views, markings) over filters or hidden columns in the application.

When a scenario separates cannot open the app from opens but shows no data, prefer checking resource sharing and group membership for the first and the exact data permission for the second, changing only the failing control.

quiz.q: Only the finance team may see a margin property on Product objects that everyone else can view. Which control fits?
choices: Hiding the margin column in each module
Asking non-finance users not to look at margin
Giving finance a separate copy of the module with the column visible
A property-level security control on margin at the data layer
quiz.explain: Property-level controls protect the value through every application and API; hiding a column only changes one view of data that remains readable.

quiz.q: A user opens an application successfully, but one page is empty while colleagues see data there. That page reads a different object type than the rest. What should be checked?
choices: Whether the user can open the application resource
Whether to grant the user Owner on every project the app touches
The user's access to the object type that page reads
Whether the module should be rebuilt from scratch
quiz.explain: The user can open the app, so resource access is fine; the empty page points to data access for the object type it reads, which should be fixed exactly.

days.recap: Enforce visibility in the data layer with markings, object and property policies or restricted views, separate opening an app from reading its data, fix only the exact failing control, and require reviewed merges with branch protection.

days.title: Execution Identity, Service Users and Operational Monitoring

concepts.heading: User-Scoped Versus Service-Identity Execution
concepts.body: The guide asks you to distinguish user-scoped and project-scoped execution and service identities. User-scoped execution runs with the invoking user's permissions, so results differ by user. Execution under a service identity uses a configured service user's access, which should be least privilege and can be restricted to selected markings; for example, a compute-module Function can run with application permissions, where a third-party application's service user determines its access. If a user-scoped function returns fewer results for a manager than expected, check the manager's permissions and decide access with the data owner instead of changing the execution mode. Never use elevated execution to work around a missing access decision.

concepts.heading: Controlled Writes Under a Service Identity
concepts.body: Some writes are intentionally ones users must not perform directly, such as creating records in a restricted audit object type. A function-backed Action that writes under a scoped service identity lets users invoke the Action without holding edit rights on the audit type. Cross-project reporting can use a least-privilege identity that reads the sources and writes only to a restricted reports project. Because elevated execution creates objects, check where it writes and the permissions on the created objects, so outputs are not visible to people who should not see them. Document the identity, its minimal permissions, what it writes where, who can see the output and who owns it.

concepts.heading: Automations and Identity Continuity
concepts.body: Automations run as their owner, so an automation owned by an employee who leaves can start failing when that person's access ends. The durable fix is ownership by a team-controlled, least-privilege service user, such as a scoped third-party application. When a service identity's permissions are reduced or an automation moves to a new identity, grant exactly what the workflow needs, for example the missing write permission, and test. After credential rotation, update references and verify the identity kept its permissions. An automation creating tasks the triggering user cannot see is expected behaviour when documented, not a bug.

concepts.heading: What to Monitor
concepts.body: An application's health spans several components: Action failures, Function errors and latency, automation failures and missed runs, Ontology indexing health and lag, backing data freshness, and AIP usage and errors. If apps show outdated values for up to an hour after successful builds, check indexing health and latency, because built data must be indexed before applications show it. If a nightly rebuild sometimes finishes late, monitor freshness and alert the owner before business hours. Alerts should route to the owning team's rotation with a runbook, so failures at 03:00 are found within minutes rather than at 09:00. A component-level health summary helps operations leads each morning.

concepts.heading: Diagnose With Evidence and Keep Alerts Useful
concepts.body: When an AI-assisted application becomes slow, use per-component monitoring and traces to find which step's latency or errors changed before changing anything. If Actions time out at month end, correlate with operational signals; a monthly batch automation causing contention can be rescheduled or throttled. If AI costs double, examine per-feature usage, call counts and tokens per call. Sixty constantly firing alerts get ignored and hide real outages, so review every alert: keep the actionable ones, tune thresholds, merge duplicates and assign owners. Good monitoring is owned, actionable and reviewed regularly.

examPoints: When a scenario needs users to trigger writes they must not make directly, prefer an Action or Function running under a least-privilege service identity whose writes and outputs are documented, rather than granting users edit rights.

When a scenario reports applications lagging behind successful builds, slowing down or failing at certain times, prefer component-level signals (indexing lag, data freshness, Function latency, automation runs, AIP usage) routed to owners over guessing at fixes.

quiz.q: A nightly automation that closes stale tickets stopped working in the week its owner moved to another department and lost access to the ticket project. What is the durable fix?
choices: Restore the former owner's access to the ticket project
Move ownership to a team-controlled, least-privilege service user
Grant the automation organization-wide administrator rights
Retire the automation and close stale tickets by hand
quiz.explain: Automations run as their owner, so a personal owner ties them to one person's access; a scoped, team-controlled service user keeps them running with least privilege.

quiz.q: After each successful nightly build, a dashboard keeps showing the previous day's figures for about 40 minutes and then catches up. What should be checked first?
choices: The users' browser settings
The Action's submission criteria
The OSDK package version
Ontology indexing health and latency for the object type
quiz.explain: Built data must be indexed before applications show it, so a lag after successful builds points to indexing; the other options do not affect read freshness.

days.recap: Know whose permissions each execution uses, put controlled writes behind least-privilege service identities owned by teams, and monitor Actions, Functions, automations, indexing, freshness and AI with owned, actionable alerts.

days.title: Final Review: Exam Strategy and Cross-Domain Judgement

concepts.heading: Exam Format and Pacing
concepts.body: The Application Developer – Associate exam has 85 multiple-choice questions in 3 hours, and the pass mark is 70% correct. It is open-book, and certificates are valid for two years; after a fail there is a 14-day wait before a retake. The guide lists eight domains but publishes no domain weights, so this course gives each domain equal time. Three hours for 85 questions is a little over two minutes per question, enough to read every scenario carefully. Use the time to find the evidence in each stem rather than to look up trivia.

concepts.heading: Stay Inside the Developer's Role
concepts.body: The exam guide separates what the application developer owns from what they do not primarily own. Keyed answers stay inside the developer's work: modelling the Ontology for a workflow, Actions, Functions, Workshop, the OSDK, automations, AI features and application security. Options that move the problem to another role, rebuild upstream systems or skip governance are often distractors. When two answers seem plausible, prefer the one a developer can do safely within their own scope. Role awareness also helps you recognize when the right step is a decision with a data owner, such as marking membership.

concepts.heading: The Simplest Safe Option From Evidence
concepts.body: The guide rewards diagnosing from evidence before changing anything, then making the narrowest change that fixes the cause. Wrong answers repeat familiar patterns: rebuild first, grant broad access, use a bigger model, add a longer prompt or more context, hide data with silent filters, remove validation, overwrite production, or hide slowness behind a spinner. Right answers use the evidence available, such as execution history, evaluation and effect history, traces, lineage and monitoring signals. Read each stem for the clue that narrows the cause, such as only some users, only some objects, or since yesterday's change. Then pick the option that fixes exactly that.

concepts.heading: Patterns That Cross Domains
concepts.body: Several ideas recur in every domain. Idempotency protects Action webhooks, automation effects, bulk OSDK calls and generated functions from duplicates. Server-side filtering and aggregation keep functions, Workshop modules and external apps fast and correct. Versioning and stable interfaces apply to functions, embedded modules and OSDK packages, with consumers migrated deliberately. Data-level security beats interface tricks everywhere, and Workflow Lineage comes before any change to shared resources.

concepts.heading: Assigning Each Need to the Right Component
concepts.body: Many questions are really about choosing the right component. The Ontology holds the model (objects, links, interfaces, shared properties); Actions make governed writes with criteria and permissions; Functions hold reusable logic in TypeScript v2 or Python v2; AIP Logic handles language tasks with typed outputs; Workshop serves internal interfaces and the OSDK serves custom or external ones; Automate handles follow-ups and scheduled work. Security comes from roles, markings and data policies, with branch protection on production changes. In your final days, revisit the exam points of each domain and practise scenarios where these responsibilities blur. If you can say why each wrong option belongs to a different component or role, you are ready.

examPoints: When two answers both seem to work, prefer the one that diagnoses from evidence and changes the narrowest control or component, over broad grants, rebuilds, bigger models or removing protections.

When a scenario spans several layers, prefer assigning each part to its proper tool: the Ontology for the model, Actions for governed writes, Functions for logic, Workshop or the OSDK for the interface, Automate for follow-ups and AIP Logic for language tasks.

quiz.q: A user cannot run an Action, and a teammate suggests granting the user Owner on every related project. Which response fits the guide's approach?
choices: Grant Owner now and remove it later
Remove the Action's submission criteria
Find the exact layer that denies the user and change only that
Rebuild the module that shows the Action
quiz.explain: The guide favours diagnosing the failing permission and fixing it narrowly; broad grants and removed validation trade one problem for a bigger one.

quiz.q: Which pairing of requirement and component is correct?
choices: Preventing approvers from approving their own requests: conditional visibility in Workshop
Computing an exact tax amount: an AIP Logic prompt
Sending a confirmation email after an approval: an automation
Restricting salary to HR: hiding the column in the module
quiz.explain: Post-decision follow-ups are automation work; self-approval needs submission criteria, exact tax needs deterministic code, and salary needs data-level property controls.

days.recap: Pace for about two minutes per question, stay within the developer's role, choose the simplest safe option the evidence supports, and assign each need to its proper component.
